title: Law, Art, Science and Charity
bigQuestion: How have the world's religions shaped the laws people live under, the buildings and music they make, the way they study nature, and the way they care for strangers?

story.title: Three Doors, Three Communities
story.kicker: A hospital, a food pantry and a school, each opened by a community of faith, and each open to anyone who walks through the door.
paragraphs: In 1852 a small group of Catholic nuns, the Sisters of Mercy, opened the first chartered hospital in Chicago. The city was young, muddy and crowded, and cholera swept through it more than once. The sisters nursed patients who could not pay and patients who did not share their faith. They kept records, trained nurses and begged for donations. Mercy Hospital served Chicago's South Side for more than 160 years. Its founders said they were doing what their tradition asked: to visit the sick and care for the stranger.

On a Saturday morning on Chicago's Southwest Side, volunteers at a mosque line up paper bags on folding tables. Rice, lentils, canned tomatoes, a bag of onions, a box of cereal. The money came partly from zakat, the yearly share of wealth that Muslims give to those in need, and partly from voluntary gifts. The line outside includes Muslim families, a Mexican grandmother with a wire cart, and a retired man from the block who has never set foot inside the prayer hall. No one asks anyone what they believe.

Outside a town in Punjab, India, a Sikh congregation pooled donations for years and built a school. The classrooms have ceiling fans and a computer lab. At noon the students file into the langar, the free kitchen that every gurdwara keeps, and sit in long rows on the floor to eat lentils and flatbread. Hindu, Muslim and Sikh children sit side by side. The volunteers who cook and serve call their work seva, service done for its own sake and not for pay or praise.

Three communities, three traditions, three doors that stay open to outsiders. Each community would tell you it is following its own text: the words of Jesus about feeding the hungry, the Qur'an's command to give, the Sikh Gurus' teaching about equality and service. This chapter follows religion out of the house of worship and into the wider world. It looks at four places where religion and culture meet: law, art, science and the care of people in need. In each, the traditions differ, and in each, they have left marks you can still see.
story.think: Each of the three communities serves people outside its own faith. Why might a religious text ask its followers to do that, and what would a community gain or lose by serving only its own members?

lessons.title: Hammurabi's Stone and Sinai's Law
lessons.mainIdea: Ancient Near Eastern law codes and the Torah's laws share forms and topics, but the Torah presents its law as the terms of a covenant with God.
reading: A black stone pillar more than seven feet tall stands in the Louvre in Paris. It was carved for Hammurabi, king of Babylon, around 1754 BCE. At the top, the king stands before Shamash, the Babylonian sun god who oversaw justice, and receives from him the symbols of authority. Below are about 282 laws about wages, contracts, marriage, theft and injury. This is the *Code of Hammurabi*, one of the oldest law collections in the world. From the very beginning, law and religion were carved on the same stone.

The Torah, the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, also contains law, mainly in Exodus, Leviticus and Deuteronomy. In the biblical story, God gives these laws to Moses at Mount Sinai as the terms of a *covenant*, a binding agreement between God and the people of Israel. Scholars have noticed that some of the Torah's laws resemble Hammurabi's. Both deal with an ox that gores a person, and both use the formula of *lex talionis*, a Latin phrase meaning the law of retaliation: an eye for an eye. The Torah's framing is different, though. Its law is presented as a relationship, not only a royal decree, and it returns again and again to the stranger, the widow and the orphan.

How a law is read matters as much as what it says. In Jewish tradition, the rabbis of the Talmud read an eye for an eye as a rule of fair compensation, meaning the value of an eye, not the taking of one. Jewish tradition counts 613 commandments, or *mitzvot*, in the Torah, and the body of law worked out from them is called *halakha*, a Hebrew word meaning the way one walks. Christians read the same laws through the New Testament. Many Christians hold that the Torah's moral commands still bind them while its ritual laws were fulfilled in Jesus. Jews and Christians share the text but not the way of reading it.

words.d: a collection of about 282 laws carved on a stone pillar for the king of Babylon around 1754 BCE
a binding agreement; in the Hebrew Bible, the bond between God and Israel sealed at Sinai
Latin for the law of retaliation, the principle of an eye for an eye found in Hammurabi's code and the Torah
commandments; Jewish tradition counts 613 of them in the Torah (singular: mitzvah)
Jewish law as worked out by the rabbis from the Torah; the word means the way one walks

look.title: The Law of Retaliation
look.text: And if any mischief follow, then thou shalt give life for life, Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, Burning for burning, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.
look.prompt: Jewish tradition has long read this passage as a rule of fair compensation rather than literal injury. How does knowing how a community reads a law change what the law means in practice?

check.q: What is the Code of Hammurabi?
choices: A collection of about 282 Babylonian laws carved on a stone pillar around 1754 BCE
The first five books of the Hebrew Bible
The rabbis' commentary on the Torah's laws
A Roman legal code adopted by the early church
check.why: The Code of Hammurabi is the Babylonian king's law collection, carved on a stone pillar now in the Louvre.

check.q: What does lex talionis mean?
choices: The law of the covenant
The law of retaliation, an eye for an eye
The 613 commandments
The way one walks
check.why: Lex talionis is Latin for the law of retaliation; it appears in both Hammurabi's code and the Torah.

check.q: How did the rabbis of the Talmud read the phrase an eye for an eye?
choices: As a command to be carried out literally by the courts
As a law that applied only to kings
As a rule of fair compensation for the value of the injury
As a law that Christians replaced
check.why: Jewish tradition read the formula as requiring payment equal to the injury, not the taking of an eye.

lessons.title: Sharia and the Schools of Law
lessons.mainIdea: Sharia is what Muslims understand as God's guidance for life; fiqh is the human scholarship that works it out, and that scholarship has several schools.
reading: In a courtyard at al-Azhar in Cairo, one of the oldest centers of Islamic learning, students sit in circles around a teacher and argue about a case. What if a traveler cannot find water for washing before prayer? What makes a sales contract fair? These are questions of *sharia*. The Arabic word originally meant a path to water. For Muslims, sharia is the whole of God's guidance for how to live, covering worship, family, business and conduct. The human effort to understand that guidance is called *fiqh*, which means understanding. Muslim scholars, the *ulama*, have always distinguished the two. Sharia is understood as God's; fiqh is human work that can be debated and revised.

Sunni scholars traditionally draw on four sources. The first is the Qur'an. The second is the *Sunnah*, the example of the Prophet Muhammad, known through the hadith, the reports of his words and actions. The third is consensus among qualified scholars. The fourth is reasoning by analogy. For example, the Qur'an forbids wine. Later scholars reasoned that other intoxicating substances share the same harm and so fall under the same rule. Over the centuries, four major Sunni schools of law took shape: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali, each strongest in different regions. Twelver Shia Muslims follow the Ja'fari school. The schools differ on many details, such as the exact posture in prayer, and have generally recognized one another as valid.

A qualified scholar may issue a *fatwa*, a legal opinion in answer to a question. A fatwa is advice, not a court order, and a Muslim may seek a second opinion. Today most Muslim-majority countries use national law codes for crime and commerce, and sharia-based law applies mainly to family matters such as marriage and inheritance. How far religious law should shape state law is debated among Muslims themselves, with a wide range of views. In the United States, Muslims follow sharia in personal life, such as prayer, fasting and halal food, in the same way that observant Jews follow halakha, under the civil law that governs everyone.

words.d: in Islam, God's guidance for all of life; the word originally meant a path to water
Islamic jurisprudence, the human scholarship that works out what sharia requires
Muslim religious scholars trained in the Qur'an, hadith and law
the example of the Prophet Muhammad, known through the hadith, a source of Islamic law
a legal opinion issued by a qualified Muslim scholar in answer to a question; it is advice, not a court ruling

look.title: Two Scholars, One New Question
look.text: A new energy drink arrives in a city in the year 1250. Nothing in the Qur'an or the hadith mentions it. One scholar says: the Qur'an forbids wine because it clouds the mind; this drink does the same, so the same rule applies. A second scholar says: the drink does not cloud the mind, only speeds the heart, so it is permitted, though perhaps unwise. Both scholars use the same four sources.
look.prompt: Which of the four sources of Sunni law is each scholar using, and why can two careful scholars reach different answers from the same sources?

check.q: How do Muslim scholars distinguish sharia from fiqh?
choices: Sharia is Shia law and fiqh is Sunni law
Sharia is understood as God's guidance, while fiqh is the human effort to understand it
Sharia covers worship and fiqh covers business
Sharia is the Qur'an and fiqh is the hadith
check.why: Sharia is God's guidance as Muslims understand it; fiqh, meaning understanding, is the human scholarship that works it out.

check.q: Which is one of the four traditional sources of Sunni law?
choices: The rulings of the caliph
The Talmud
Reasoning by analogy from a known case
A vote of the whole community
check.why: Sunni scholars draw on the Qur'an, the Sunnah, the consensus of scholars and reasoning by analogy.

check.q: What is a fatwa?
choices: A binding court sentence
One of the four Sunni schools of law
A chapter of the Qur'an about law
A scholar's legal opinion given in answer to a question
check.why: A fatwa is a qualified scholar's opinion; it is advice, not a court order, and a person may seek another view.

lessons.title: Canon Law, Halakha and the First Amendment
lessons.mainIdea: Religious communities keep their own internal law, such as canon law and halakha, while the U.S. Constitution keeps government from establishing or restricting religion.
reading: Around 1140 a monk in Bologna named Gratian gathered thousands of church rulings that seemed to contradict one another and tried to reconcile them. His book, the *Decretum*, became the foundation of *canon law*, the law of the Christian church. The word canon comes from a Greek word for a measuring rule. Church councils had issued canons since the Council of Nicaea in 325. Today the Catholic Church's Code of Canon Law, issued in 1917 and revised in 1983, governs the sacraments, the clergy, marriage cases and church courts. Orthodox churches follow ancient canons as interpreted by their synods. Protestant churches have their own governing documents, such as a Book of Discipline or a Book of Order.

Jewish communities have long kept a parallel system. A *bet din*, a rabbinic court of three judges, rules on conversion, on religious divorce and on disputes that the parties agree to bring before it. Orthodox, Conservative and Reform Jews differ on how binding halakha is and on who may interpret it. In medieval Europe, church courts, Jewish courts and royal courts operated side by side, and a person might live under two or three legal systems at once. That world of overlapping laws is the background to the American arrangement.

In 1791 the United States adopted the First Amendment. It says that Congress shall make no law respecting an *establishment* of religion or prohibiting the *free exercise* of it. An established church is an official one, supported by the state; England still has one, and several American states kept establishments into the 1800s, Massachusetts until 1833. Under the First Amendment, religious communities are free to run their own law inside their own communities. A bet din or a church court can decide who is a member in good standing. But civil courts do not enforce religious law, and religious law cannot override civil law. A religious wedding still needs a civil license, and no religious court can fine or jail anyone.

words.d: the internal law of a Christian church; the word canon comes from a Greek word for a measuring rule
Gratian's collection of church law, made around 1140 in Bologna, the foundation of later canon law
a Jewish religious court of three judges that rules on matters such as conversion and religious divorce
an official state church supported by the government; the First Amendment forbids Congress to create one
the right to practice one's religion, protected by the First Amendment

look.title: The First Amendment
look.text: Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.
look.cite: First Amendment to the United States Constitution, ratified 1791
look.prompt: Which words in this sentence keep the government from having an official religion, and which words keep it from punishing people for practicing one? Why might both be needed?

check.q: What did Gratian do around 1140?
choices: He wrote the Code of Canon Law of 1917
He founded the first Jewish court in Europe
He gathered and reconciled contradictory church rulings into the Decretum
He drafted the First Amendment
check.why: Gratian, a monk in Bologna, compiled the Decretum, which became the foundation of canon law.

check.q: What is a bet din?
choices: A Catholic church court
A Protestant governing document
A state court that enforces religious law
A Jewish religious court of three judges
check.why: A bet din is a rabbinic court that rules on matters such as conversion and religious divorce.

check.q: Under the First Amendment, what can a religious court in the United States do?
choices: Decide who is a member in good standing of its own community
Fine or jail a member who breaks religious law
Perform marriages without a civil license
Overrule a civil court's decision
check.why: Religious communities may run their own internal law, but religious law cannot override civil law or impose punishments.

lessons.title: Buildings That Teach
lessons.mainIdea: Sacred architecture puts a tradition's beliefs into stone: which way you face, where the light falls and who may enter all carry meaning.
reading: Step inside a traditional Hindu temple and the building leads you inward. Past the porch and the pillared hall is a small dark room called the *garbhagriha*, a Sanskrit word meaning womb chamber, where the image of the deity is kept. A tower rises above it, often shaped like a mountain peak, because many Hindus picture the gods dwelling on Mount Meru at the center of the world. Worshipers walk clockwise around the shrine, a practice called pradakshina. Buddhist builders used a different form, the *stupa*, a solid mound built over relics, which pilgrims also circle. In East Asia the stupa became the tiered pagoda.

In medieval Europe, Christians built to bring in light. At Chartres Cathedral in France, mostly complete by about 1220, pointed arches and outside supports called *flying buttresses* carry the weight of the roof. That freed the walls for enormous windows of colored glass. Church leaders such as Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis taught that light was a symbol of God. The windows told Bible stories to people who could not read, and the floor plan formed a cross. Orthodox Christians favored a central dome, with an image of Christ as ruler of all painted at its top. Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, finished in 537, is the great example. It became a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934 and a mosque again in 2020.

A mosque is built around a direction. One wall, the *qibla* wall, faces Mecca, and a niche in it, the *mihrab*, marks the direction of prayer. Beside it stands the minbar, a stepped pulpit for the Friday sermon. A tower, the *minaret*, carries the call to prayer, and a fountain in the courtyard serves for washing before prayer. There are no statues or pictures of people; the decoration is geometric pattern and calligraphy from the Qur'an. The prayer hall is open floor, so that rows of worshipers can stand shoulder to shoulder. A Sikh gurdwara, by contrast, is defined by openness. The Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the Golden Temple, has four doors, one on each side, which Sikhs understand as a welcome to people of every caste and faith.

In Wilmette, Illinois, on the lakefront north of Chicago, stands the Bahá'í House of Worship, dedicated in 1953. It is the oldest surviving Bahá'í temple in the world. It has nine sides and nine doors, because the number nine symbolizes unity and completeness in the Bahá'í faith. Its lacework dome is made of concrete and crushed quartz. Like the mosque's qibla wall or the temple's inner chamber, its shape is a teaching. When you read a sacred building, ask three questions: Which way does it face? Where does the light go? Who is invited in?

words.d: the small inner chamber of a Hindu temple where the deity's image is kept; the word means womb chamber
a Buddhist mound built over relics, which pilgrims walk around; the ancestor of the pagoda
an outside stone support that carries a Gothic church's roof weight, freeing the walls for windows
the direction of Mecca, which Muslims face in prayer; the qibla wall of a mosque faces it
the niche in a mosque wall that marks the direction of Mecca
the tower of a mosque from which the call to prayer is given

lessons.title: Images, Icons and Empty Space
lessons.mainIdea: Traditions disagree about whether the sacred may be pictured, and their art, from icons to calligraphy to empty niches, shows the answer each one gives.
reading: The Ten Commandments in Exodus forbid making a graven image. Jewish tradition has read this as a ban on images of God, and synagogue art has usually used symbols instead: a menorah, lions, a crown for the Torah. Yet an ancient synagogue at Dura-Europos in Syria, from the third century CE, had wall paintings of biblical scenes, so the rule was not always applied the same way. Islam takes a similar path. The Qur'an condemns idols, and many hadith discourage pictures of living beings, so mosques are decorated with *calligraphy*, geometric pattern and vines. This avoidance of images is called *aniconism*. It was never total. Persian and Mughal artists painted people in books, and sometimes even the Prophet, usually with his face veiled.

Christians argued about images for more than a century. In Orthodox Christianity an *icon* is a painted image of Christ, Mary or a saint, and believers say it is a window toward heaven. They venerate it with a kiss or a bow but say they worship God alone. Between 726 and 843 the Byzantine emperors twice tried to destroy icons, a movement called *iconoclasm*, meaning image-breaking. The Second Council of Nicaea in 787 ruled that veneration of images was right. In the sixteenth century the argument returned. Reformers such as Zwingli and Calvin removed images from churches, while Luther kept many, and Catholic churches remained full of statues and glass.

Hindu practice goes further in the other direction. A *murti* is an image of a deity into which, through a ceremony, the deity is invited to be present. Worshipers offer it flowers, food and light. Hindus explain that they are not worshiping a statue; the image is a form through which the formless can be approached. Buddhist art tells a story of change. The earliest Buddhist carvings, at Sanchi in India in the first century BCE, never showed the Buddha's body. They showed his footprints, an empty seat or the tree he sat under. Around the first and second centuries CE, sculptors in Gandhara and Mathura began carving the Buddha in human form, and those images spread across Asia.

words.d: the avoidance of images of God, people or living beings in religious art
the art of beautiful writing; in Islamic art, verses of the Qur'an written as decoration
in Orthodox Christianity, a painted image of Christ, Mary or a saint that believers venerate
image-breaking; the Byzantine movement of 726 to 843 that destroyed icons, and later Protestant removal of images
a Hindu image of a deity, understood as a form through which the deity is present and worshiped

look.title: No Graven Image
look.text: Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
look.prompt: Which communities in this lesson read this verse as a full ban on religious images, and which read it more narrowly? Give one example of each from the reading.

check.q: What is aniconism?
choices: Painting icons on wooden panels
The avoidance of images of God or living beings in religious art
The ceremony that invites a deity into a murti
The destruction of images by emperors
check.why: Aniconism is the avoidance of images; Islamic art's use of calligraphy and pattern is the clearest example.

check.q: What did the Second Council of Nicaea decide in 787?
choices: That icons must be destroyed
That only calligraphy could decorate churches
That veneration of images was right
That statues were allowed but paintings were not
check.why: The council of 787 ruled in favor of venerating icons, against the iconoclasts.

check.q: How did the earliest Buddhist art at Sanchi show the Buddha?
choices: As a seated figure in meditation
As a standing king
As a face painted on a dome
Through symbols such as footprints, an empty seat or a tree
check.why: Early Buddhist carvings avoided the Buddha's body; human images appeared later in Gandhara and Mathura.

lessons.title: Chant, Recitation and Song
lessons.mainIdea: In most traditions the sacred text is heard as much as read, and sound carries it: chant, recitation, kirtan and gospel song.
reading: Psalm 150 lists trumpet, harp, drum, strings and cymbals and tells everything that breathes to praise God. The Hebrew Bible describes choirs of Levites singing in the Temple in Jerusalem. In the synagogue today a cantor chants the Torah using *cantillation*, a system of marks written above and below the words that tell the reader how each phrase rises and falls. Christian monks sang the Psalms daily. The plain, unaccompanied melody of the Western church became known as *Gregorian chant*. It is named for Pope Gregory I, around 600, though it was written down centuries later. Luther wrote hymns for congregations to sing. Bach composed cantatas for Lutheran services, and Orthodox churches still sing without instruments.

The word Qur'an means recitation, and Muslims hear the text far more often than they see it. A trained reciter follows *tajwid*, the rules for pronouncing every letter and pause, and recitation contests draw large audiences. Many Muslims do not call this music, and the distinction matters to them. Sikhs sing their scripture. The hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib are arranged by musical mode, and *kirtan*, devotional singing with harmonium and drum, fills a gurdwara for hours. Hindus sing bhajans and kirtan to Krishna, Rama and the Goddess, a practice that the saint Chaitanya spread through Bengal in the sixteenth century. Buddhist monks chant sutras, and Tibetan monks are known for a deep, layered chant.

Chicago gave the world a new sacred music. In 1932 Thomas A. Dorsey, a blues pianist who had turned to church music, began directing the choir at Pilgrim Baptist Church on the South Side. That year, after the deaths of his wife and infant son, he wrote Precious Lord, Take My Hand. He joined the harmonies of the spirituals to the rhythm of the blues, and the result was *gospel music*. Mahalia Jackson, who had moved to Chicago from New Orleans in 1927, became its most famous voice. In 1963 she sang at the March on Washington just before Martin Luther King Jr. spoke. Gospel spread from Chicago's Black churches to the whole world.

words.d: the chanting of the Torah in the synagogue, guided by marks that show how each phrase rises and falls
the plain, unaccompanied chant of the Western Christian church, named for Pope Gregory I
the rules for the correct pronunciation and pacing of Qur'an recitation
devotional singing of scripture or hymns in Sikh and Hindu practice, usually with instruments
a form of Christian sacred music that grew out of Black churches in Chicago in the 1930s, joining spirituals and blues

look.text: Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp. Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs. Praise him upon the loud cymbals: praise him upon the high sounding cymbals.
look.prompt: Orthodox Christians sing without instruments, and many Muslims do not call Qur'an recitation music at all. How could communities that honor this psalm reach such different practices?

check.q: What is cantillation?
choices: Singing hymns with a harmonium in a gurdwara
Reciting the Qur'an in competition
The chanting of the Torah guided by marks above and below the words
The blues-based church music of Chicago
check.why: Cantillation is the synagogue chanting of the Torah, guided by written marks.

check.q: Which tradition's scripture is arranged by musical mode and sung as kirtan?
choices: The Catholic Mass
The Buddhist sutras
The Hebrew Psalms
The Sikh Guru Granth Sahib
check.why: The hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib are arranged by musical mode and sung as kirtan in the gurdwara.

check.q: What did Thomas A. Dorsey do at Pilgrim Baptist Church in Chicago?
choices: He joined spirituals and blues to create gospel music
He wrote the first Gregorian chants in America
He introduced Qur'an recitation contests
He translated the Psalms into English
check.why: Dorsey directed the choir there from 1932 and blended spirituals with blues rhythm, creating gospel music.

lessons.title: Observatories and Scriptoria
lessons.mainIdea: For centuries religious needs and religious institutions drove much of the world's science, from Islamic astronomy and algebra to monastic and university scholarship in Europe.
reading: Islam gave its scholars mathematical problems to solve. Muslims pray five times a day at times set by the sun, so they needed accurate tables of sunrise, noon and dusk. They pray facing Mecca, so they needed to calculate that direction from any city on a round earth. Their calendar follows the moon, and the shares of an inheritance are set in the Qur'an as fractions. In Baghdad in the early 800s the caliph al-Ma'mun supported the *House of Wisdom*, where scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic. There al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on solving equations whose title gave us the word *algebra*; his own name became the word algorithm. Muslim astronomers refined the *astrolabe*, a brass instrument for finding the time and the stars. Ibn al-Haytham tested how light and vision work with experiments, and Ibn Sina's medical textbook was taught in Europe for centuries.

In Christian Europe the monastery was the library. Benedict's Rule, written around 530, set monks to prayer and work, and the work often meant copying books by hand in a room called the *scriptorium*. Monks preserved Roman and Greek texts that would otherwise have vanished. The English monk Bede, who died in 735, worked out the calculation of the date of Easter, a science called *computus*, and popularized counting years from the birth of Jesus. Cathedral schools grew into the first universities, at Bologna, Paris and Oxford, because the church needed trained clergy and lawyers. Much later, Gregor Mendel, a friar in Brno, bred pea plants in the monastery garden and founded genetics with a paper published in 1866. Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian priest and physicist, proposed in 1927 that the universe is expanding, the idea that became the Big Bang.

Other traditions have their own stories. Indian mathematicians such as Brahmagupta, writing in 628, developed rules for zero and negative numbers, and the oldest Indian geometry appears in texts about building Vedic altars. The Buddhist monk Yi Xing measured the length of a degree of the earth's meridian for the Tang court in the 720s. Jesuit missionaries ran the imperial astronomy bureau in Beijing in the 1600s. The Jewish philosopher Maimonides was a physician to the sultan's court in Cairo. For most of these people, studying nature was a religious act. Psalm 19 says the heavens declare the glory of God, and many scholars in the Abrahamic traditions took that as an invitation to look closely.

words.d: a center of translation and scholarship in Baghdad in the 800s, supported by the Abbasid caliphs
the branch of mathematics for solving equations, named from the title of al-Khwarizmi's book
a brass instrument used by medieval astronomers to find the time, the stars and the direction of Mecca
the room in a monastery where monks copied books by hand
the medieval science of calculating the date of Easter

look.title: Seven Old Places of Learning
look.cite: commonly cited dates; several are approximate and debated by historians
look.prompt: Every one of these schools began inside a religious institution. What did each tradition need educated people for, and how might that shape what was taught?

choices: To predict harvests for zakat

To set the five daily prayer times and find the direction of Mecca
To translate Greek texts
check.why: Prayer times follow the sun and prayer faces Mecca, so astronomy and geometry were religious needs.

check.q: What was a scriptorium?
choices: A monastery's chapel
A tool for measuring stars
A school for training lawyers
The room where monks copied books by hand
check.why: The scriptorium was the copying room; monks there preserved many ancient texts.

check.q: Who founded genetics with pea-plant experiments published in 1866?
choices: Gregor Mendel, a friar in Brno
Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian priest

Al-Khwarizmi, a Baghdad mathematician
check.why: Mendel bred peas in his monastery garden; Lemaitre later proposed the expanding universe.

lessons.title: Galileo and the Church
lessons.mainIdea: The Galileo affair of 1616 to 1633 was a conflict over who may interpret Scripture and nature, not a simple war between religion and science.
reading: In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus, a Catholic church official in Poland, published a book arguing that the earth moves around the sun. He dedicated it to the pope, and for decades it caused little stir. Then, in 1609 and 1610, Galileo Galilei pointed a telescope at the sky. He saw four moons circling Jupiter and saw Venus go through phases like the moon. Both fit a sun-centered system far better than the old earth-centered one. Galileo was a devout Catholic whose two daughters became nuns, and at first church astronomers in Rome welcomed his discoveries.

The trouble was the Bible. Verses such as Joshua's command to the sun to stand still, and a psalm that says the world cannot be moved, seemed to place the earth at rest. After the Protestant Reformation, the Catholic Church had ruled at the Council of Trent that individuals must not interpret Scripture against the agreed reading of the early church fathers. In a 1615 letter, Galileo argued that the Bible teaches how to reach heaven, not how the heavens move. In 1616 church officials declared *heliocentrism* contrary to Scripture and told Galileo not to hold or defend it. In 1632 he published a Dialogue that clearly defended it anyway. In 1633 the Roman *Inquisition* tried him, found him vehemently suspect of heresy, and made him *recant*. He lived under house arrest until his death in 1642, and his book stayed on the *Index of Forbidden Books* until 1835.

The story is more tangled than a simple fight between faith and reason. Some Protestant leaders had also rejected Copernicus. Jesuit astronomers went on doing careful science, and the Church never condemned mathematics or observation as such. Historians point to politics, personal quarrels and the pressures of the Thirty Years' War. In 1992 Pope John Paul II accepted the report of a commission that acknowledged the errors of the theologians who judged Galileo. The affair remains the classic case for one question: when a reading of a sacred text and a finding about nature seem to conflict, who decides, and how?

words.d: the view that the earth and planets move around the sun, proposed by Copernicus in 1543
a Catholic church court that tried cases of heresy; the Roman Inquisition tried Galileo in 1633
to formally take back a statement or belief, as Galileo was made to do

lessons.title: Darwin and the Range of Responses
lessons.mainIdea: Religious responses to Darwin's theory of evolution have ranged from rejection to full acceptance, and that range exists inside every major tradition.
reading: In November 1859 Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species. He argued that living things change over vast time through *natural selection*: individuals with helpful traits survive and reproduce more, so species slowly change and new ones arise. In 1871 he applied the idea to human beings. Religious readers split at once. Charles Kingsley, an Anglican priest, wrote to Darwin that a God who made creatures able to develop themselves was as noble as one who made each separately, and Darwin quoted him in the next edition. Asa Gray, a Harvard botanist and devout Presbyterian, defended Darwin in America. Charles Hodge of Princeton Seminary answered in 1874 that Darwinism, by removing design, amounted to atheism.

In the United States the argument moved into the schools. The *fundamentalist* movement, named for a set of pamphlets published between 1910 and 1915, defended the literal truth of the Bible. In 1925 Tennessee banned the teaching of human evolution, and a teacher named John Scopes was tried in Dayton that July in a trial that drew reporters from around the world. He was convicted and fined. In 1968 the Supreme Court ruled such bans unconstitutional. Today American Christians hold a range of views. Young-earth *creationism* reads Genesis as literal history and dates the earth to a few thousand years. Old-earth creationists accept the age of the earth but not common descent. *Theistic evolution* accepts the science fully and holds that God works through it.

The range runs through other traditions too. In 1950 Pope Pius XII permitted Catholics to study the evolution of the human body, and in 1996 John Paul II said the theory was more than a hypothesis. Most Reform and Conservative Jews and many Orthodox Jews accept evolution; some in the strictest communities do not. Among Muslims opinion is divided. A ninth-century scholar in Baghdad, al-Jahiz, wrote about animals changing to fit their surroundings, while in 2017 Turkey removed evolution from its high school curriculum. Many Hindu and Buddhist thinkers find long ages and changing forms easy to accept. The Dalai Lama has written that he accepts evolution but questions whether it is truly random. The lesson is that no tradition speaks with one voice on this.

words.d: Darwin's mechanism of evolution: individuals with helpful traits survive and reproduce more, so species change over time
a Protestant movement, named for pamphlets of 1910 to 1915, that defends the literal truth of the Bible
the view that God created living things directly as described in Genesis; young-earth creationists date the earth to a few thousand years
the view that evolution happened as science describes and that God works through it

lessons.title: Zakat and Tzedakah
lessons.mainIdea: In Islam and Judaism, giving to the poor is an obligation of justice rather than an optional kindness: zakat and tzedakah.
reading: Before the Eid prayer that ends Ramadan, every Muslim household that can afford it gives a small gift of food or money so that the poor can celebrate too. That is one form of *zakat*, the third of the Five Pillars of Islam. The main zakat is yearly. Muslims who hold savings above a set minimum for a year give about 2.5 percent of that wealth. The Qur'an, in chapter 9, names who may receive it: the poor, the needy, those who collect it, new Muslims, captives, people in debt, those working in God's cause and stranded travelers. Beyond zakat, Muslims give *sadaqa*, voluntary charity of any size. Wealthy Muslims have long set up a *waqf*, an endowment whose income funds a mosque, a school, a hospital or a public fountain forever.

The Hebrew word for charity, *tzedakah*, comes from tzedek, which means justice. In Jewish tradition, giving is a debt owed, not a favor granted. The Torah commands farmers to leave the corners of their fields and the fallen grain for the poor and the stranger, which is how Ruth gathers food in the book named for her. A *tithe*, a tenth of one's produce or income, is set aside. Many Jewish homes keep a small box for coins to give away. In the twelfth century, the philosopher Maimonides ranked eight levels of tzedakah. The lowest is giving grudgingly. Near the top is giving so that neither giver nor receiver knows the other. The highest of all is a loan, a partnership or a job that lets the person no longer need help.

The two systems share a shape. Both make giving a duty of justice rather than a mood of pity. Both protect the dignity of the receiver: the Qur'an warns against spoiling a gift with reminders and insults, and Maimonides prizes anonymity. Both build institutions. Christians took over the tithe as a standard for church giving, and the weekly collection remains a fixture of most congregations. Today zakat flows through organizations such as Islamic Relief, and Jewish federations gather tzedakah for schools, elder care and emergencies. The Jewish Federation of Metropolitan Chicago, founded in 1900, is one of the oldest in the country.

words.d: the yearly share of wealth, about 2.5 percent of savings, that Muslims must give to those in need; the third pillar of Islam
voluntary charity in Islam, given beyond the required zakat
an Islamic endowment whose income permanently supports a mosque, school, hospital or other public good

a tenth of one's produce or income set aside for religious and charitable purposes

lessons.title: Charity, Seva and Dana
lessons.mainIdea: Christianity, Sikhism, Hinduism, Buddhism and Confucianism each teach giving and service in their own terms: charity, seva, dana and ren.
reading: In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus describes a final judgment in which the king says that whoever fed the hungry, welcomed the stranger, clothed the naked and visited the sick and imprisoned did it to him. Christians call these the works of mercy. The English word charity comes from the Latin *caritas*, which means love, and the King James Bible uses charity to translate the love that Paul praises in 1 Corinthians 13. The early church appointed deacons to distribute food to widows. Benedict's Rule told monks to receive every guest as Christ. In modern times, William Booth founded the Salvation Army in London in 1865, Dorothy Day began the Catholic Worker houses in 1933, and Mother Teresa founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata in 1950.

Sikhs call service *seva*, and the plainest form of it is the *langar*, the free kitchen attached to every gurdwara. Guru Nanak began the practice in the early 1500s, and the third Guru, Amar Das, made it a rule that anyone who came to see him, rich or poor, must first eat in the langar. Everyone sits in rows on the floor, because no one is higher than anyone else. The langar at the Golden Temple in Amritsar feeds tens of thousands of people every day, and every meal is cooked and served by volunteers. Sikhs are also asked to give a tenth of their income, called dasvandh. Since 1999 the Sikh charity Khalsa Aid has carried the langar idea into disaster zones and refugee camps.

In Hinduism and Buddhism the word for giving is *dana*. Each morning in Thailand, Sri Lanka and Myanmar, Buddhist monks walk through the streets with bowls, and laypeople place cooked food in them. The gift feeds the monks, and Buddhists teach that it also earns *merit*, good karma that shapes the giver's future. Hindu temples serve free meals to all comers; the temple at Tirupati in South India feeds enormous crowds daily. Buddhist Tzu Chi, founded in Taiwan in 1966 by the nun Cheng Yen, is now one of the largest charities in Asia. Confucian teaching speaks of *ren*, usually translated as humaneness. The Analects sum it up as not doing to others what you would not want done to yourself. Mencius added that anyone who sees a child about to fall into a well feels alarm, and that this feeling is the seed of humaneness.

words.d: Latin for love; the source of the English word charity, used in the King James Bible for Christian love
selfless service in Sikh teaching, done without pay or desire for praise
the free community kitchen of a Sikh gurdwara, where all eat together seated in rows on the floor

lessons.title: Hospitals, Schools and Relief
lessons.mainIdea: Many of the world's hospitals, schools and relief agencies began as religious institutions, and many still are, serving people of every faith and none.
reading: The word hospital shares a root with hospitality. Around 370 Basil, the bishop of Caesarea in what is now Turkey, built a complex outside the city to house and treat the sick and the poor. In the Islamic world the *bimaristan*, a Persian word meaning place of the sick, appeared in Baghdad and Cairo by the 800s and 900s. The hospital founded in Cairo by Ahmad ibn Tulun in 872 treated patients free of charge, and later bimaristans had separate wards for fevers, wounds and mental illness, all funded by waqf endowments. Medieval Europe's hospitals were run by religious orders. Chicago's own story begins with the Sisters of Mercy in 1852. Today religious health systems remain large; by one estimate about one in seven hospital patients in the United States is treated in a Catholic hospital, and Jewish, Methodist, Lutheran, Baptist and Adventist hospitals serve millions more.

Schools followed the same path. The *madrasa*, a college of Islamic learning, spread across the Muslim world after the founding of the Nizamiyya in Baghdad in 1065. Christian cathedral schools became universities. In 1780 Robert Raikes opened a Sunday school in England to teach reading to working children. In the United States, Catholic *parochial schools*, run by parishes, grew into one of the largest private school systems in the country, with Chicago's among the biggest. Jewish day schools, Sikh Khalsa schools and Buddhist temple schools in Thailand tell the same story. The record is not all bright. Missionary schools spread literacy but often served colonial powers, and in the United States and Canada, church-run boarding schools separated Native children from their families and languages.

Modern disaster relief is heavily religious in origin. The American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee began in 1914 to aid Jews caught in the First World War. The Quakers' American Friends Service Committee, founded in 1917, shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1947. Catholic Relief Services dates from 1943, World Vision from 1950, Islamic Relief from 1984, and the Sikh Khalsa Aid from 1999. Such *faith-based organizations* are among the largest aid groups in the world. They also raise a hard question: should aid ever be tied to religion? In 1994 the Red Cross and major relief agencies, including many religious ones, adopted a code of conduct promising that aid would not be used to promote a political or religious point of view.

a college of Islamic learning, especially of law and theology
